title: The Linux Directory Tree
lead: In Linux everything has its place: fixed directories for configuration, logs, user files and programs. Learn where to look for which file.
objectives: You explain that Linux has no C: or D: drive and everything branches under one root directory `/`.
You tell apart the roles of `/etc`, `/home`, `/root`, `/var/log`, `/usr`, `/bin`, `/dev`, `/tmp`, `/proc` and `/opt`.
You move safely through the system with `ls`, `cd` and `cat` and build the "ID card" of a server.

sections.title: The root of the tree: /
body: Windows has drives like `C:` and `D:`. Linux has just **one** tree whose root is `/` (the root directory). Even a new disk or USB stick is **mounted** onto a branch of this tree.

Where things live is defined by the **FHS** (Filesystem Hierarchy Standard). That is why you find config files in the same place on Ubuntu and Rocky. You see the root directory with `ls /`; you change nothing by doing so.
Quick map: `/etc` configuration, `/home` users, `/var` variable data (logs), `/usr` programs, `/tmp` temporary files, `/proc` and `/sys` virtual kernel files, `/dev` devices.

commands.what: Lists the folders inside the root directory.
commands.where: When you first enter a system.
commands.why: You get to know the main branches of the tree.

commands.where: As the starting point for absolute paths.
commands.why: Paths starting with `/` work from anywhere.

commands.what: Prints the full path of the current directory.
commands.where: After navigating, to be sure where you are.
commands.why: Prevents actions in the wrong directory.

sections.tip: A path starting with `/` is **absolute** (`/etc/hostname`); without it, the path starts in the current directory.

sections.title: Configuration and users: /etc, /home, /root
body: `/etc` holds the **configuration files** of the system and installed programs: `/etc/passwd` (users), `/etc/hostname` (machine name), `/etc/fstab` (disks), `/etc/os-release` (distribution). They are plain text files you read with `cat`.
Personal files of normal users live under `/home/<user>`, for example `/home/student`. The administrator `root` has its own home, `/root`; only root may enter, others get `Permission denied`.
`/etc/shadow` stores password hashes and is readable by root only. `cat /etc/shadow` as a normal user fails; that is not a fault but protection.

commands.what: Shows the name and version of the distribution.
commands.where: To find out which Linux you are on; same path on every distribution.
commands.why: You pick the right commands for that distribution.

commands.where: When working with several servers, to confirm you are on the right one.
commands.why: Reduces the risk of working on the wrong server.

commands.what: Lists the home directories of normal users.
commands.where: To quickly see which users exist.
commands.why: You see where user data lives.

sections.tip: Always make a backup before changing a config file; in this module you only read.

sections.title: Logs and virtual files: /var, /proc, /sys
body: `/var` holds data that **changes** while the system runs. Most important is `/var/log`: system and service logs live here. On RHEL, Rocky and Alma the main log is `/var/log/messages`, on Ubuntu it is `/var/log/syslog`. Do not look for logs in `/etc`: configuration is in `/etc`, logs in `/var/log`.

`/proc` and `/sys` are not real files on disk. The kernel generates them in RAM on the fly. The numbers in `ls /proc` are the IDs of running processes (PIDs). `cat /proc/cpuinfo` shows live CPU data, `cat /proc/meminfo` memory data.
Use these files for **reading** only. Browsing around in them or writing to them is not a safe habit.

commands.where: The first place to look when troubleshooting.
commands.why: You follow the trail of a problem in the logs.

commands.what: Reads the CPU information from the kernel.
commands.why: As a virtual file it is always up to date.

commands.what: Searches for files by name below a directory.
commands.where: When you do not know which directory a file is in.
commands.why: Instead of guessing, you find the exact path.

sections.tip: Is the file called `messages` or `syslog`? It depends on the distribution; look first with `ls /var/log`.
sections.danger: Writing to files under `/proc` and `/sys`, or opening `/proc/kcore` with `cat`, can make the system unstable. Only read known files such as `cpuinfo`, `meminfo` or `version`.

sections.title: Programs and devices: /usr, /bin, /dev, /tmp, /opt
body: `/usr` is the big library of installed programs. Most commands live in `/usr/bin`. On modern distributions `/bin` is not a separate directory but a **symbolic link** (symlink) to `/usr/bin`: `ls -ld /bin` shows `bin -> usr/bin`.
`/dev` holds device files: `/dev/sda` is a disk, `/dev/null` is a "black hole" that swallows everything written to it. In `ls -l` their lines start with `c` (character device) or `b` (block device).

`/tmp` is for temporary files and is usually cleared on reboot. `/opt` is for third-party software, `/srv` for data the server publishes. If you cannot find an application, look in `/opt`, `/usr/local` and `/etc` in turn.

commands.what: Shows the `/bin` entry itself; the link target appears after `->`.
commands.where: To tell whether a path is a directory or a link.
commands.why: Explains why the tree can look different between distributions.

commands.what: Shows the type and permissions of a device file.
commands.where: When examining how hardware appears as a file.
commands.why: You see that in Linux everything is a file.

commands.what: Lists the directory for third-party software.
commands.where: When looking for a manually installed application.
commands.why: Software outside the package manager often lives here.

sections.tip: To learn where a command lives, you can type `which ls`.
sections.warn: `/tmp` is accessible to everyone. Do not store secrets such as passwords there, and read the path twice before using `rm -r` even in `/tmp`.

t10.hint: `/root` is only the home of root.

t11.hint: Logs are not under `/etc` but under `/var`.

t12.text: Mini project: build a small FHS tree under `~/mini-root`. With one `mkdir -p` create the folders `etc`, `var/log` and `tmp`, create the file `etc/app.conf` with `touch`, and write a log line with `echo started > ~/mini-root/var/log/app.log`.
t12.hint: Braces: `~/mini-root/{etc,var/log,tmp}`; you write into the log file with the redirect `>`.

t13.text: Challenge: write the server's ID card into `~/idcard.txt`: machine name (`/etc/hostname`), users (`ls /home`) and distribution name (the `PRETTY_NAME` line). Use `>` for the first, `>>` for the others.

t14.text: Challenge: you do not know the path of `sshd_config`. Search for it by name under `/etc`: `find /etc -name sshd_config`.
t14.hint: `-name` expects the file name; the path turns out to be under `/etc/ssh/`.

t15.text: TICKET #2410 — "The shop application (`shopapp`) reports errors and we can find neither its install location nor its logs." The third-party software is under `/opt`. Find the `ERROR` line in its log file and save it to `~/ticket-2410.txt`.

vm.intro: In this section you only read; no command changes system files. Output may differ slightly by distribution (Ubuntu / Rocky / Alma / WSL); that is normal.

v01.title: Explore the root directory
v01.text: List the contents of the root directory and paste the output.

blocks.expected: bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var

differs: The number and order of folders depend on the distribution; `etc`, `var` and `usr` must appear.
If the output is a single column, widen the terminal; the content is the same.

v02.title: Which distribution am I on?
v02.text: Read the distribution info and paste the output.
differs: On Ubuntu you see `NAME="Ubuntu"` and `ID=ubuntu`; the lines differ but `NAME=` and `ID=` are always there.
If the file is missing the system is very old; try `cat /etc/issue`.

v03.title: Is /bin really a link?
v03.text: List `/` in long format and look at the `bin` line.
differs: If the output is empty try `ls -ld /bin`; on very old distributions `/bin` is a real directory.
If the line starts with `l` it is a symbolic link.

v04.title: Virtual files: /proc
v04.text: Read the first lines of the kernel's CPU information.
differs: On ARM CPUs (UTM on Apple Silicon) the fields differ; the `processor` line still appears.
On WSL the contents of `/proc` may be somewhat restricted.

v05.title: Look at the log directory
v05.text: List the log files and paste the output.

blocks.expected: anaconda  audit  dnf.log  messages  secure  wtmp ...

differs: On Ubuntu you see `syslog` and `auth.log`, on Rocky `messages` and `secure`.
Some files need `sudo` to read; listing does not.

v06.title: A file in the temporary directory
v06.text: Create a test file in `/tmp`, look at it and delete it right away. Deleting a single file is safe.
differs: If you mistyped the name, `rm` says "No such file"; the name must be `lab-test.txt`.
Do not use `-r` or wildcards (`*`) with `rm`.

v07.title: A device file
v07.text: List `/dev/null` in long format and paste the output.
differs: If the line starts with `c` it is a character device; other permission letters are no problem.
If the file is missing you may be in a container; a normal VM always has it.

q1.q: In which directory do you look for system logs?
q1.explain: Logs are constantly growing data and live under `/var/log`. `/etc` is for configuration files.

options: Because only root may see it
They are not real files on disk; the kernel generates the information in RAM
Because it is downloaded from the internet
q2.explain: `/proc` and `/sys` are a live interface of the kernel and take no disk space.

q3.q: In which directory are the configuration files of the system and programs?
q3.explain: `/etc` is the standard place for configuration files (`passwd`, `hostname`, `fstab`...).

q4.q: Where are the personal files of `student`, and where those of `root`?
q4.explain: Normal users live under `/home/<name>`; root's home is separately `/root`.

summary: Linux has a single tree; the root is `/` and everything hangs below it.
`/etc` configuration, `/var/log` logs, `/home` and `/root` home directories, `/usr` programs.
`/proc` and `/sys` are virtual kernel files; `/dev` is for devices, `/tmp` for temporary files, `/opt` for third-party software.
When searching, first think about what a directory is for, then verify with `ls`, `cat` and `find`.

glossary.meaning: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: defines what each directory is used for.
The top of the tree, `/`; all paths branch from here.
A full path starting with `/`, independent of where you are.
A special file pointing to another path; shown with `->` in `ls -l`.
The numeric ID of each running process; appears as a directory name under `/proc`.
